transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because it’s gotten really hard for me to be near heights at work — like scaffolds, roof edges, upper platforms, that kind of thing. I’m a construction manager, so it’s not exactly something I can just avoid easily.

What happens is, even when I can see the guardrails are there, and I know the setup is supposed to be safe, my head just keeps telling me I’m about to go over the edge. It’s like I know logically that everything’s in place, but the second I get close, my mind starts screaming that I’m going to fall. It’s been bad enough that I figured I needed to come talk to someone, because it’s really interfering with what I’m supposed to be able to do.
Is it just heights that trigger this kind of fear, or are there other situations that make you feel similarly anxious?

It’s really the heights, yeah. I mean, specifically when I’m near something like a scaffold, a roof edge, or one of the upper platforms on a job site. That’s when it kicks in hard.

It’s not even that I look at it and think, “Oh, this is objectively unsafe,” because a lot of the time I can see the rails are there, I know the setup has been checked, I know how these things are supposed to be built. I’ve been around construction long enough to understand that. But once I’m close to the edge or up on that level, my head just goes straight to, “You’re going to go over.” Like I’m about to fall, even when there’s no real reason for me to think that in the moment.

So, no, I wouldn’t say it’s a bunch of different situations. It’s mainly those height situations at work that set it off.
How often do you experience this fear when you're near heights at work?

Pretty much every time I’m actually near those height situations at work. It’s not like I can predict one day will be fine and another won’t — if I step onto temporary stairs, or even just start walking toward an open upper floor, it hits right away.

I mean, the second I’m in that situation, my chest tightens up, my hands get wet, and I get this feeling like my legs might lock before I can make myself take another step. It’s not some slow build where I have time to talk myself out of it. It’s immediate, like my body reacts before I’ve even fully thought it through.
Do you experience this intense fear or anxiety when you're not near heights, such as in your daily life or in other situations that don't involve being at a high place?

No, not really. I mean, I don’t walk around all day feeling that same kind of fear in regular situations. It’s not like going to the grocery store or being at home or driving around town makes me feel like that.

It’s specifically when I have to get near height-related stuff at work — a scaffold, a roof edge, an upper platform, that kind of thing. That’s when it happens. Even if I can look right at the guardrails and know, as a construction guy, that they’re there for a reason and the setup is supposed to be safe, my head just goes straight to, “You’re about to go over.” It feels very automatic. Outside of those situations, I wouldn’t say I have that same intense fear.
Has your fear of heights at work affected your relationships with family or friends?

With family and friends… I mean, not in the obvious way, I guess. It’s not like I’m snapping at people at home all the time or avoiding my friends because of them. But it has definitely spilled over, because work has gotten tense, and then I carry that home.

The bigger thing is at work itself. I’ve missed or put off enough of the upper-level walk-throughs that people have noticed. My crews, some of the subcontractors, they’ve started questioning my calls more, like they’re wondering why I’m sending someone else up or why I’m not checking something myself. And that’s… embarrassing, honestly, because I’m supposed to be the one making those decisions and doing those safety inspections.

It got to the point where my employer’s insurer pushed for an occupational health review because I wasn’t completing some of the key safety inspections. So, yeah, that kind of pressure affects everything around me. I go home thinking about it, feeling like I’m losing credibility, and I’m sure my family sees that stress on me.
Are there any situations outside of work where you avoid doing something because of your fear of heights?

Outside of work… honestly, not much comes to mind. The avoidance is really tied to the job, because that’s where I’m expected to go up and inspect things or make decisions from upper levels.

At work, though, I’ve definitely been avoiding it. I’ve been handing off height inspections to my foremen when I can, or I’ll move meetings that were supposed to happen upstairs or on an upper deck down to ground level instead. I can usually make it sound practical, like it’s more efficient or we can see the plans better in the trailer, but the real reason is I don’t want to go up there.

And when I absolutely have to go up, I don’t like going alone. I’ll keep someone right beside me, almost like I need them there as a backup, and then I rush through whatever I’m supposed to check. I’m still scared the whole time, but I just try to get it over with as fast as possible.
Are there any activities you enjoy or used to enjoy that you now avoid because of your fear of heights?

Yeah… I guess the main “activities” I’ve stopped doing are work-related ones, more than like hobbies or weekend stuff. I don’t really have, you know, rock climbing or anything like that that I used to enjoy and now don’t do.

But at work, there are things I used to just do as part of the job without making a whole production out of it. Height inspections, walking an upper level, checking something from a roof edge or scaffold — I used to be able to just go handle it. Now I find ways around it. I’ll hand those inspections off to my foremen if I can, or I’ll change a meeting that was supposed to happen upstairs and move it down to ground level. I can usually justify it, like, “Let’s meet in the trailer, it’ll be quicker,” but I know what I’m doing.

And if I absolutely have to go up, I don’t like being up there by myself. I keep somebody right next to me, and then I rush through the whole thing. I’m trying to look calm and do my job, but inside I’m scared the whole time and just thinking, “Get this done and get back down.” So, yeah, it’s less about fun activities and more that I’m avoiding parts of the job I used to be able to do normally.
Are you finding that your fear of heights is affecting how you spend your free time or leisure activities?

I’m not really sure that it has, at least not in a clear way. Like, I can’t think of some hobby or weekend activity that I’ve stopped doing because of heights. Most of my free time is pretty normal, I guess — family stuff, errands, trying to unwind when I’m not at work.

I mean, if you asked whether I’m going out looking for high places in my spare time, no, definitely not. But I don’t think I was ever doing that much anyway, so it’s hard to say it’s changed my leisure activities. The place where it really shows up is work, because that’s where I’m expected to go up on things. Outside of that, I haven’t really noticed it controlling my free time in the same way.
Do you ever experience this fear of heights when you're not at work, even if it's just a slight feeling?

Yeah… I mean, I’d say it’s mostly at work, but the feeling itself isn’t like it only exists because I’m on a job site. If I’m near an edge or up on something high, even if it’s not technically “dangerous,” my mind kind of does the same thing.

The clearest version is still when I’m near a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform — that’s where it really hits me. I can look right at it and see there are rails, I can know in my head that the setup is supposed to be safe, and still there’s this immediate thought like, “I’m going to go over.” Not like I want to or anything — it’s more like my brain suddenly tells me that’s what’s about to happen, even when the logical part of me knows it doesn’t make sense.

So outside of work, it might just be a smaller version of that if I’m somewhere elevated, but the strongest and most obvious place it happens is around those work situations. That’s really why I’m here, because every time I have to get near those areas now, it’s like my body and my head react before I can talk myself out of it.
Does your fear of heights ever occur in situations that are not related to your job as a construction manager?

Yeah, it can, but the way I’ve been thinking about it is that work is just where it gets put in front of me the most. I mean, I’m not usually choosing to be around heights on my own time, so it doesn’t come up as often outside the job.

But the fear itself isn’t really about “construction,” if that makes sense. It’s when I get near something like a scaffold, a roof edge, an upper platform — that kind of setup. Even if I can look at it and see the rails are there, and I know in my head it’s supposed to be safe, my mind still does this thing where it tells me I’m about to go over. Like, not that I want to, just that I’m going to lose control or somehow end up over the edge.

That’s really why I’m here. It’s not just me being cautious at work. Every time I have to get near those kinds of places now, my head reacts before I can reason with it. So outside of work, if I were in the same kind of height situation, yeah, I think it would happen there too.
Are there any everyday activities, outside of work, that you avoid because they might involve being in a high place?

Yeah… I mean, outside of work, not as much in the sense of hobbies or social stuff, because honestly I don’t put myself in those situations if I can help it. But the avoiding is definitely happening — mostly around the work-related height stuff, even though I know you asked everyday life.

Like, I’ve been handing off inspections that involve heights to my foremen more than I probably should. If something needs to be checked up high, my first move now is to see if someone else can go do it and report back to me. And I’ll move meetings or walkthroughs to ground level whenever I can, even if it’s a little awkward or makes me look like I’m being overly particular.

When I absolutely have to go up, I don’t like doing it alone. I’ll make sure someone is right beside me, almost like I need them there as a guardrail even if there’s already a guardrail, if that makes sense. And then I just rush through whatever I’m supposed to do — I’m not calmly inspecting or taking my time. I’m just trying to get it done and get back down, and I’m scared the whole time.
When you're in a high place outside of work, like a balcony or a mountain overlook, do you experience the same level of fear as you do at work?

Yeah… I think it would be the same kind of fear, if I’m actually near the edge. I guess the reason I keep talking about work is because that’s where it happens over and over, and where I can’t really just choose not to deal with it.

But it’s not like the fear is only about the job site itself. The thing that sets it off is being near that kind of drop — like a scaffold, or a roof edge, or an upper platform. I can be standing there and see the rails are in place, and I can know, logically, that the setup is supposed to be safe, but my head still tells me I’m about to go over. It feels automatic, like the thought gets there before I can argue with it.

So with something like a balcony or an overlook… if I’m back from the edge, maybe I can manage it better, but if I had to stand right there near the drop, I think it would be the same reaction. That “I’m going to go over” feeling. That’s the part that scares me, because it doesn’t seem to matter that I know better.
Do you experience this fear of heights in your personal life, outside of work-related situations, as intensely as you do at work?

Yeah… if it’s the same kind of situation, then yes, it can feel just as intense. I know I keep coming back to the work examples, but that’s because that’s where I run into it the most. It’s not like my fear is about paperwork or being on a job site or supervising crews — it’s specifically when I have to get near something like a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform.

That’s really why I’m here. Every time I have to get near one of those places now, my head tells me I’m about to go over. Even when I can see the rails are there, even when I know the setup is supposed to be safe, it doesn’t really calm me down the way it should. I can tell myself, “This is built for this, people are up here all the time, you know what you’re doing,” but there’s this immediate reaction like I’m about to lose control or somehow end up over the side.

So outside of work, if I’m in that same position — near the edge, up high, with that drop there — I don’t think my body or my mind really makes a distinction. Work just forces me into it more often.
Do you think you would experience this fear of heights if you were to encounter a high place in a completely personal, non-work context, such as on vacation?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, if I were on vacation and ended up somewhere high — like not even a worksite, just some place with a drop-off — I don’t think my mind would care that I’m “off the clock,” you know?

The main thing is that edge, or being up on something where there’s space below me. That’s why I keep saying I’m here because every time I have to get near a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform now, my head immediately tells me I’m about to go over. And it does that even when I can see the rails are there, even when I know the setup is supposed to be safe.

So if I was on vacation and there was, say, some viewing platform or a balcony or something like that, and I had to get close to it, I’d expect the same reaction. Maybe the surroundings would be nicer, but the fear would still be the same. It’s the height and the drop that sets it off.
Would you say your fear of heights is something that you experience equally in both work and personal life situations, or is it more prominent in one over the other?

It’s more prominent at work, just because that’s where I’m forced to deal with it the most. I mean, in my personal life I can usually choose not to walk up to the edge of something, or I can hang back and let other people go look, or I just avoid those situations without making a big thing of it.

But the fear itself… I don’t think it’s different. It’s not like the job is what scares me. It’s when I have to get near a scaffold, or a roof edge, or an upper platform — that’s when my head tells me I’m about to go over. And that happens even when I can see the rails are in place, even when I know the setup is supposed to be safe. I can understand it logically, but it doesn’t stop that immediate reaction.

So I’d say work makes it show up more, and maybe makes it feel more serious because I can’t just walk away from it. But if the same kind of height was in my personal life, near an edge or a drop, I think the fear would be the same.
Do you think your fear of heights would still be present if you were to change jobs and no longer work in construction?

Yeah, I do. I mean, I think changing jobs would probably mean I’m not running into it as constantly, so in that sense maybe I’d have fewer moments where it hits me. But I don’t think the fear itself would just disappear because I wasn’t in construction anymore.

Because what brings me in here is that every time I have to get near something like a scaffold, or a roof edge, or an upper platform, my head immediately goes to, “You’re going to go over.” It’s not really about the company or the worksite or the job title. It’s that situation of being up there with a drop nearby. Even when I can see there are rails in place, and even when I know it’s supposed to be safe, my mind still doesn’t accept it in the moment.

So if I changed jobs and never had to be around those kinds of places, I guess I could avoid it more easily. But if I ended up on a balcony, or a high platform, or anything like that, I’d expect the same thing to happen. It feels like the job exposes it, but it didn’t create the fear.
If you were to find yourself in a high place outside of work, such as a balcony or a mountain overlook, and you couldn't avoid it, would you experience the same level of fear as you do at work?

Yeah… if I couldn’t avoid it, I think it would be the same level, honestly. Maybe at work it feels more intense because I’m expected to keep functioning and make decisions and not look shaken, but the actual fear — the thing that hits me — I think that would be the same.

Like, if I’m on a balcony or a mountain overlook and I have to be near the edge, my head doesn’t really care whether it’s work or not. It goes straight to, “You’re going to go over.” That’s the part that scares me so much, because even if I can see there’s a railing, even if I know it’s built to be safe and other people are standing there fine, I still get that feeling like I’m not safe up there.

That’s really why I’m here. Every time I have to get near a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform now, it’s like my brain just locks onto the drop and tells me something bad is about to happen. So outside of work, if it was the same kind of height and I couldn’t back away from it, yeah, I’d expect the fear to be just as bad.
Would your fear of heights still be present in situations where you are not at work and there is no professional expectation for you to be in a high place?

Yes, it would. I don’t think the work part is what creates it, if that makes sense. Work just puts me in front of it more often and makes it harder to step away without it becoming a problem.

But even if there were no job involved, no one expecting me to be up there, I still think I’d react the same way if I had to be near a drop. Like, if I’m close to a roof edge, or a scaffold, or some upper platform — even when I can see the rails are there, even when I know in my head that the setup is supposed to be safe — my brain just immediately tells me I’m about to go over. It’s not a rational thought exactly, but it feels real in the moment.

So yes, outside of work, if I was in that kind of high place and couldn’t just avoid it or back away, the fear would still be there. The pressure at work makes it more noticeable, but the fear itself isn’t limited to work.
Do you think your fear of heights would be considered a problem if it weren't affecting your work?

Honestly… I don’t know that I would’ve come in if it wasn’t affecting work, because I probably would’ve just kept avoiding heights and told myself it was fine. But I do think it would still be a problem, just maybe easier for me to hide from.

The reason it’s gotten impossible to ignore is that it’s now interfering with things I’m supposed to be doing. I’ve missed or delayed enough upper-level walk-throughs that my crews and subcontractors have started questioning my calls. And that’s hard to admit, because in my position I’m supposed to be the person checking things, making decisions, making sure the job is moving safely. When I hesitate or push something off because it involves going up to a higher level, people notice.

It’s gotten to the point where my employer’s insurer pushed for an occupational health review because I wasn’t completing key safety inspections. So, if it weren’t affecting work, maybe I’d be less pressured to deal with it. But the fear itself would still be there. Work is just where the consequences have become really obvious.
